title: Are We Merely Practising Democracy as a System of Governance, or Are We Truly Living Democracy as a Constitutional Commitment?
author: Sreejata Ghosh
excerpt: A Constitution Day reflection on whether democracy is merely a system of governance or a commitment to dignity, freedom, equality and accountability.

content.text: Every year on November 26, we celebrate Constitution Day. We share quotes by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, hoist flags, organize panel discussions, and remind ourselves that we belong to the world’s largest democracy. Yet, amidst all the ceremonial pride, one uncomfortable question refuses to leave my mind: Are we merely practising democracy as a mechanical system of governance, or are we truly living democracy as a constitutional commitment?

This question isn't born out of cynicism; it arises from looking closely at our reality. A constitution is not a museum artifact meant to be admired once a year. When Dr. B.R. Ambedkar and the Constituent Assembly drafted the Constitution of India after independence, they didn't just write a rulebook for running elections or passing bills. They handed over a living promise to the citizens of this country—a shield meant to protect the dignity, freedom, and life of every single individual.
Today, however, knowing about the Constitution has replaced respecting it.

Look around at what happens when ordinary people, especially the younger generation, step out to demand their basic rights. During peaceful Gen Z protests and citizen demonstrations, we have repeatedly witnessed governance turn into brute force—where young students and ordinary citizens are lathi-charged, silenced, or beaten simply for asking to be heard. Article 19(1)(a) and Article 19(1)(b) explicitly guarantee every citizen the fundamental right to freedom of speech, expression, and peaceful assembly. When the state responds to peaceful dissent with violence instead of dialogue, it isn't just suppressing a protest; it is tearing up the very articles that give a democracy its soul.

And this erosion isn't the fault of any single party or timeline. Across eras—whether under past governments or the present administration—those entrusted with safeguarding the Constitution have repeatedly hollowed it out from the inside.

Consider the moral contradiction we live with every day. We claim to uphold Article 14 (Equality before the law) and Article 21 (Protection of life and personal liberty, which the Supreme Court has repeatedly affirmed includes the right to live with human dignity). Yet, what message does it send to the nation when individuals accused or convicted of heinous crimes against women are rewarded with positions of immense power—made ministers, lawmakers, or appointed to high constitutional offices like Governors? When power shields predators while victims fight endless battles for basic justice, the rule of law becomes a cruel joke.

Ask yourself: what value does a constitutional promise hold when a missing child or a missing woman cannot be traced within the crucial first twenty-four hours? How do we reconcile our celebratory speeches with the grim reality of rising crimes against women, sexual violence, domestic abuse, and human trafficking? Article 15(3) empowers the state to make special provisions for the safety and upliftment of women and children, and Article 51A(e) places a fundamental duty on every citizen to renounce practices derogatory to the dignity of women. Yet, policy after policy fails to guarantee the most basic right of all: the right to walk safely on the street or feel secure inside one’s own home.

The tragedy is twofold. First, those sitting in positions of power—the lawmakers, the administrators, the custodians of our institutions—have treated the Constitution as an obstacle to be bypassed rather than a covenant to be honored. They take oaths in its name, yet their actions routinely betray its spirit. Second, as citizens, we have grown dangerously numb. We treat constitutional rights as privileges granted by politicians rather than birthrights earned through sacrifice.
“However good a Constitution may be, if those who are implementing it are not good, it will prove to be bad.”
content.attribution: Dr. B.R. Ambedkar, final speech to the Constituent Assembly, November 25, 1949

content.text: So, on this Constitution Day, before we post celebratory graphics or recite the Preamble, we need to ask the people sitting in power—and ourselves—some hard questions:

items: If the state cannot protect a citizen's life, dignity, and right to dissent, what are we celebrating?
If constitutional offices can be occupied by those who violate the law, who is left to defend it?
Are we protecting the Constitution, or are we slowly dismantling it while keeping its cover intact?

content.text: Celebrating Constitution Day means nothing if the Constitution only lives on paper while dying on our streets, in our police stations, and in our corridors of power. True patriotism isn't blind applause; it is holding the custodians of our democracy accountable to every single word Dr. Ambedkar wrote for us. Until the last woman feels safe, until the missing are found, and until a citizen can question power without fear, our democracy remains unfinished business.

title: Navnirman Youth Parliament 2.0 — Registration
